items.title: 国际原子能机构促伊朗恢复核查
items.summary: 国际原子能机构周五向成员国散发报告，要求伊朗恢复核查人员进入其核设施的通道，称这对履行监督伊朗核计划的职责至关重要。报告表示，缺乏伊朗核设施与核材料的信息“令人担忧核扩散”，需以最高紧迫性纠正，并特别关注伊斯法罕附近一处地下铀浓缩厂。据美联社报道，该机构称已完全准备好在短时间内恢复保障监督活动。伊朗外交部发言人巴加埃周一称，伊朗仍致力于履行《不扩散核武器条约》，并将合作受限归咎于美以袭击。

IAEA chief Rafael Grossi has called on Iran to restore access to its nuclear facilities [File: Joe Klamar/AFP]

By AFP, AP and Reuters

Published On 13 Nov 202613 Nov 2026

The United Nations nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to allow it to resume inspections of its nuclear facilities.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for Tehran to restore access for its inspectors in a report circulated by the watchdog among member states on Friday, insisting the move is essential to carry out its remit to monitor the Iranian nuclear programme.

Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel launched attacks on the country’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. The report said Tehran had told the organisation that it was not possible to allow the inspections to continue amid the current security situation.

The IAEA said the lack of information about Iran’s atomic sites and nuclear material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” The Associated Press news agency reported.

The watchdog noted that it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice”.

The report expressed particular concern about an underground uranium-enrichment plant near Isfahan in central Iran, according to the Reuters news agency.

Tehran declared the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant in 2025 but has not permitted the IAEA access to inspect the facility.

Inspectors still do not know the plant’s precise location, whether it holds nuclear material, or its status under international monitoring rules. The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place there.

Advertisement

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible and help restore routine monitoring, the AFP news agency said.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.

But he blamed US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA. Since the bombing of the nuclear facilities last year, the watchdog has been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium, the report noted.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with it.

The IAEA’s inspections are intended to verify that nuclear material is not diverted towards weapons. Without direct access to sites such as Isfahan, the agency cannot independently establish what is happening at those facilities.

However, the report notes that Iran told the IAEA this month that discussion on resuming inspections in the country cannot resume amid “persistent, explicit, and public threats by the President of the United States of America … to commit further acts of armed aggression”.

Iran said that the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored,” the report added.

BEIJING: China warned the United States on Friday (Nov 13) against putting additional export controls on semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia.

China "has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party's interests," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing when asked about calls from US lawmakers to impose more limits on exports of chip equipment to China.

"China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations," Mao said.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang - who resigned on Thursday - has admitted to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

Reports allege the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping reroute restricted Nvidia technology to China.

US media quoted US lawmakers as saying that they were in favour of imposing additional export controls on chips to China as a result of the snowballing scandal.

"The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here. I'm in favour of limiting those exports," House speaker Mike Johnson was quoted as saying.

"I think there is a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take."

US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging that Alice Huang - no relation to Jensen Huang - was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.

Beijing has rejected the allegations and on Thursday said that they are a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology.

The furore comes ahead of a meeting expected next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen in southern China at an APEC gathering.

Asylum seekers caught in US immigration crackdown

By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters

Published On 13 Nov 202613 Nov 2026

The United States government has reported a historic high in deportations and arrests this fiscal year, surpassing previous records.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Wednesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) carried out 483,200 deportations and more than 491,000 immigration arrests in 2026.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

• list 1 of 4Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data

• list 2 of 4On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote

• list 3 of 4US lawmakers ask Trump administration to stop deportation of Afghans

• list 4 of 4Surging ICE raids shadow final weeks of California congressional race

end of list

The total number of deportations breaks all records in ICE’s 23-year history, including the previous record of 442,640 deportations made in 2025.

The report comes days after US President Donald Trump acknowledged his administration’s immigration crackdown may have been “too tough”.

“Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE’s history in terms of arrests,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

ICE said it made more than 48,000 arrests in September, ending a two-month run of record highs that reached 50,925 in August.

Vague figures?

“There is no question the administration has increased enforcement more than any prior president. There’s also evidence that the illegal immigrant population has declined significantly because of increased out-migration due to a fear of enforcement,” Steven Camarota, director of research for the Washington, DC-based Center for Immigration Studies (CIS), told Al Jazeera.

However, he highlighted ambiguity in the figures DHS released.

“Of course the data is always incomplete and it’s difficult to measure. On the specific numbers released today, the big issue that I have not been able to determine is what percentage of these individuals are interior enforcement and what percentage are removals from the interior of the United States and what percentage are those turned around at the border or at airport.

Advertisement

“Increased removals, sometimes called deportation, certainly can encourage more people to go home, and clearly that is a central goal of this administration,” Camarota concluded.

A guard looks on from behind the fence at the Northwest ICE Processing Centre in Tacoma, Washington [File: Lindsey Wasson/AP]

‘Too tough’

Trump has acknowledged that his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough”.

“A lot of people would say it is great but a lot of people would think it is too tough,” Trump said in a recent interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes.

Trump, however, defended his performance. “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out; I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law that was they came into the country illegally.”

Trump’s immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability, with his approval rating on the issue falling to 38 percent from 50 percent at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling.

‘We will rip ICE apart’

The Democrats appear to be gearing up to halt Trump’s immigration crackdown when they take control of Congress next year. They plan to target ICE tactics ⁠and expand paths to legal status, despite limits on ⁠how much they can achieve.

“We will investigate the administration weaponising DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies,” Bennie Thompson, a Mississippi Democrat and the soon-to-be chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, told the Reuters news agency in a statement.

At a news conference in the US Capitol with House members and newly elected representatives from southwestern border states, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, ‌said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals.

“We’re not going to be extreme,” Cuellar said, nodding to conservative voters across the US who cast their votes for Democrats.

But a number of Democratic voices sounded firmer.

“We will rip ICE apart,” Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said while celebrating her triumph in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two people during an enforcement surge in January.

Two US citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, were killed in Minneapolis, in incidents that were caught on bystander video.

Their shooting deaths have gone viral, prompting international outrage. Other footage shows masked agents deploying chemical agents and beating civilians who were documenting their activities or protesting – activities protected under the US Constitution.

Israeli strike on Gaza hospital deadliest since election

The Israeli military said the strike targeted Hamas commander Muhammad Abu Ismail, but his death has not been confirmed.

People inspect damage to Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip, Thursday, Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AP/Abdel Kareem Hana)

KHAN YUNIS, Palestinian Territories: Israeli fire killed 11 people in Gaza on Thursday (Nov 12), six of them in the bombing of Nasser hospital in south Gaza early in the day, health officials said, the deadliest single strike since Israel's elections last month.

The Israeli military confirmed the attack, saying they targeted "the commander of Hamas's Khan Yunis brigade Muhammad Abu Ismail and additional terrorists hiding inside of Nasser hospital".

The hospital, located in the southern city of Khan Yunis, confirmed the six deaths in a statement, while a doctor there said that the targeted building was the surgery ward and that nearly 30 people had been wounded.

Goher Rahbour, a British surgeon volunteering at the hospital, told AFP that a Palestinian doctor with whom he had conducted a surgery on Wednesday evening was among those killed in the strike.

"I was on my phone just doing a bit of reading and the strike occurred just after midnight. It was very loud, very quick. The building shook, there was a lot of smoke that came up," Rahbour told AFP.

The army said that Abu Ismail was "responsible for directing terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops and for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war", though it did not confirm whether he had died in the strike.

His name did not appear in a list of the victims provided by Gaza's civil defence rescue service.

Medical staff members salvage medical equipment at Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip, Thursday, Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AP/Abdel Kareem Hana)

The army accused Hamas in a statement of using the hospital as a command-and-control centre, to store weapons, and to conduct "interrogations and torture".

The group, however, denied using the facility for military purposes, saying Israel put forward "a false narrative" to justify its airstrikes.

The civil defence reported five other deaths on Thursday. One person was killed by "Israeli gunfire" near the al-Bureij camp, and another in an "Israeli drone strike" targeting a vehicle near Deir al-Balah, both in central Gaza.

Two more people were killed in an Israeli strike on a vehicle near Gaza City's Al-Shifa hospital, and one was killed in a drone strike in Jabalia in northern Gaza, bringing Thursday's death toll to 11.

Israel's military said it struck a militant in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City, but denied that the second strike took place near Al-Shifa hospital.

Israel is currently led by a caretaker government under Benjamin Netanyahu following an inconclusive election, with opposition bloc head Gadi Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a new administration.

Netanyahu - who has held power on-and-off for nearly 20 years and has led Israel throughout the war in Gaza - played up security threats to the country throughout the election period and has since called for a unity government.

People walk at Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip, Thursday, Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AP/Abdel Kareem Hana)

"WITHOUT PRIOR WARNING"

An AFP journalist at the scene of the Nasser hospital strike reported that one of the building's exterior staircases had partially collapsed and that indoors an entire floor was damaged, with broken concrete from collapsed walls mixed with broken medical equipment.

"The surgery building was bombed by F-16 aircraft without any prior warning, resulting in a large number of patients being wounded, and many patients and doctors being killed," paramedic Ezzedin Abu Sabha told AFP.

Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem called the strike a war crime, adding that the movement held the US-backed Board of Peace - in charge of overseeing Gaza's ceasefire plan that took effect in October 2025 - responsible for failing to prevent the attack.

The Board of Peace lamented in a statement the "tragic loss of life" and called for US President Donald Trump's peace plan to be implemented "immediately".

"Otherwise, we will continue to see tragedies in which Hamas alleges deliberate Israeli attacks on hospitals, Israel maintains that Hamas exploits these facilities for terrorist operations, and innocent Gazans ultimately pay the price," it said.

Israel has struck Nasser hospital on numerous occasions since the start of the war sparked by Hamas's unprecedented attack on Oct 7, 2023.

In August 2025, Israeli strikes on the hospital killed 20 people including five journalists in one day, according to the civil defence.

While the US-backed October 2025 ceasefire has largely subdued the fighting, Israel has kept up regular strikes in the territory. Both parties have accused each other of breaking the truce.

More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

During the same period, the Israeli military has reported the loss of seven soldiers, as well as one civilian contractor.

The Israeli military confirmed the attack, saying they targeted "the commander of Hamas's Khan Yunis brigade Muhammad Abu Ismail and additional terrorists hiding inside of Nasser hospital".

The hospital, located in the southern city of Khan Yunis, confirmed the six deaths in a statement, while a doctor there said that the targeted building was the surgery ward and that nearly 30 people had been wounded.

Goher Rahbour, a British surgeon volunteering at the hospital, told AFP that a Palestinian doctor with whom he had conducted a surgery on Wednesday evening was among those killed in the strike.

"I was on my phone just doing a bit of reading and the strike occurred just after midnight. It was very loud, very quick. The building shook, there was a lot of smoke that came up," Rahbour told AFP.

The army said that Abu Ismail was "responsible for directing terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops and for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war", though it did not confirm whether he had died in the strike.

His name did not appear in a list of the victims provided by Gaza's civil defence rescue service.
Medical staff members salvage medical equipment at Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip, Thursday, Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AP/Abdel Kareem Hana)

The army accused Hamas in a statement of using the hospital as a command-and-control centre, to store weapons, and to conduct "interrogations and torture".

The group, however, denied using the facility for military purposes, saying Israel put forward "a false narrative" to justify its airstrikes.

The civil defence reported five other deaths on Thursday. One person was killed by "Israeli gunfire" near the al-Bureij camp, and another in an "Israeli drone strike" targeting a vehicle near Deir al-Balah, both in central Gaza.

Two more people were killed in an Israeli strike on a vehicle near Gaza City's Al-Shifa hospital, and one was killed in a drone strike in Jabalia in northern Gaza, bringing Thursday's death toll to 11.

Israel's military said it struck a militant in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City, but denied that the second strike took place near Al-Shifa hospital.

Israel is currently led by a caretaker government under Benjamin Netanyahu following an inconclusive election, with opposition bloc head Gadi Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a new administration.

Netanyahu - who has held power on-and-off for nearly 20 years and has led Israel throughout the war in Gaza - played up security threats to the country throughout the election period and has since called for a unity government.
People walk at Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip, Thursday, Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AP/Abdel Kareem Hana)
"WITHOUT PRIOR WARNING"

An AFP journalist at the scene of the Nasser hospital strike reported that one of the building's exterior staircases had partially collapsed and that indoors an entire floor was damaged, with broken concrete from collapsed walls mixed with broken medical equipment.

"The surgery building was bombed by F-16 aircraft without any prior warning, resulting in a large number of patients being wounded, and many patients and doctors being killed," paramedic Ezzedin Abu Sabha told AFP.

Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem called the strike a war crime, adding that the movement held the US-backed Board of Peace - in charge of overseeing Gaza's ceasefire plan that took effect in October 2025 - responsible for failing to prevent the attack.

The Board of Peace lamented in a statement the "tragic loss of life" and called for US President Donald Trump's peace plan to be implemented "immediately".

"Otherwise, we will continue to see tragedies in which Hamas alleges deliberate Israeli attacks on hospitals, Israel maintains that Hamas exploits these facilities for terrorist operations, and innocent Gazans ultimately pay the price," it said.

Israel has struck Nasser hospital on numerous occasions since the start of the war sparked by Hamas's unprecedented attack on Oct 7, 2023.

In August 2025, Israeli strikes on the hospital killed 20 people including five journalists in one day, according to the civil defence.

While the US-backed October 2025 ceasefire has largely subdued the fighting, Israel has kept up regular strikes in the territory. Both parties have accused each other of breaking the truce.

More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

During the same period, the Israeli military has reported the loss of seven soldiers, as well as one civilian contractor.

Iranian nationals Mostafa Sepahvand (left) and Farhad Manesh were hired through social media. Photograph: Counter Terrorism Policing London/PA

Iranian nationals Mostafa Sepahvand (left) and Farhad Manesh were hired through social media. Photograph: Counter Terrorism Policing London/PA

Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists

Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.

Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.

Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”

Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”

Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”

Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”

The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Court artist sketches of (L-R) Shapoor Noori, who was cleared of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct, Sepahvand and Manesh. Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PA

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could not tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.

“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.

The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.

after newsletter promotion

He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.

Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner.

Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.

Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.

Sepahvand, Manesh and Noori had claimed asylum in the UK and received temporary leave to remain. None of them had regular full-time employment.

It is understood they met by chance and were then directed by Sepahvand and his contacts in Iran. There appeared to be no evidence of any wider plot.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh before sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

One dead, four wounded in downtown Washington shooting: police

WASHINGTON: A gunman shot one person dead and wounded four others in an upscale neighbourhood of downtown Washington on Thursday (Nov 12) before barricading himself in his apartment and killing himself, police said.

The shooting, which occurred about a mile north of the White House, sparked a massive police response in the nation's capital with dozens of law enforcement vehicles racing to the scene and police helicopters hovering overhead.

Jeffery Carroll, Washington's interim police chief, told reporters that the gunman had fatally shot one person in a fitness center attached to his apartment building and wounded four others before barricading himself in his apartment.

He said the man had fired at least twice at police through his apartment door before shooting himself. Police said the suspect had been pronounced dead at the scene.

The man, who was not identified, was apparently in "some sort of a conflict" with the homeowners association of the apartment building, which is located in the Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington, Carroll said.

One of the four wounded was in critical condition while the injuries to the others did not appear to be life-threatening, the police chief said.

Washington Mayor Muriel Bowser denounced what she described as a "senseless act of gun violence" and said the White House had been briefed about the incident.

The shooting occurred during the busy morning rush hour, snarling traffic as police closed off streets around the area.

Local and federal law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooting, Thursday, Nov 12, 2026, in Washington. (Photo: AP/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Some residents were evacuated by police while others were told to shelter in place.

The Washington Sun quoted a member of the VIDA Fitness gym as saying that he was on a treadmill at the workout facility when the shooting began.

Michael Carney said he heard a "pop" and then saw someone on the gym floor who had been shot in the head.

"Everyone was kind of just hiding behind planters and stuff," Carney told The Sun.

The Logan Circle neighbourhood is one of the most expensive in Washington and is known for chic restaurants and nightlife spots. It also sits a short distance from a heavy concentration of foreign embassies.

U.S. envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then see Zelenskyy in Dublin

Updated November 12, 20269:30 PM ET

Originally published November 12, 202610:26 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, greets Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, right, and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, center, during their meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, Moscow, Thursday.

Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP

hide caption

Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP

DUBLIN — U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin before heading to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Washington sought new momentum for its peace efforts.

Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv. The session in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled.

World

U.S. officials set to meet with Putin, Zelenskyy following Abu Dhabi peace talks

The talks produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced. Plans for another round of talks were announced as well, with Witkoff and Zelenskyy saying Europe will join, though they gave no details about which countries or how many.

Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin for about two hours before going to Dublin, where they met with Zelenskyy for more than an hour as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff (right), Jared Kushner, U.S. President Trump's son-in-law (left), and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speak to the media at the airport in Dublin on Thursday.

Peter Morrison/AP

hide caption

Peter Morrison/AP

Europe seeks a place at the negotiating table

Kushner said one goal of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.

In Abu Dhabi, several European security advisers were involved on the sidelines but not in the main three-way talk.

World

Former U.S. Ambassador William Taylor discusses the latest Russia-Ukraine talks

Speaking to reporters before boarding a plane to leave Moscow, Witkoff said the next round of talks has been agreed upon. Russian state TV showed Witkoff saying that "the Europeans will join at the next meeting," but he did not elaborate.

Zelenskyy in Dublin indicated the Europeans would not be on the sidelines. "Next meeting, Europe will be during negotiations, will be a negotiation team – not some way, not separately. They will have a voice," he said.

The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

Russia, meanwhile, doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.

But Washington and European capitals have sometimes seemed at odds in their diplomatic efforts. Trump has repeatedly sided with Putin, last month waiving sanctions and striking a deal to import Russian diesel, in moves that dismayed Ukraine and European leaders.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov argued that for Europe to join peace talks, it first must name a representative.

"The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism."

Many in Europe also see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat and has demanded the alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.

Putin's aide calls the talks 'constructive'

Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.

Thursday's talks were "substantive, constructive, frank and useful," Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said.

He added that the Kremlin leader reminded Witkoff and Kushner about Moscow's proposals from 2021 -- before it sent troops into Ukraine -- demanding that NATO roll back the alliance's military deployments in Central and Eastern Europe. Russia will update those with "fresh considerations," Ushakov said.

Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire — an idea long floated by Europe to prevent a new attack by Moscow — would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate target. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," the Russian president said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, second right, speaks to U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, second left, and Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, third left, as Russian Presidential foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, behind Putin, and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Special Presidential Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries Kirill Dmitriev, right, sit near during the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, in Moscow, on Thursday.

Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP

hide caption

Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP

He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.

Fighting continues as another bitter winter approaches

Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.

Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.

Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."

How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war

Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned

November 12, 20269:22 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka leaves the parliament building after submitting his resignation letter in Jakarta, Indonesia, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026.

Tatan Syuflana/AP

hide caption

Tatan Syuflana/AP

JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.

Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.

"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.

"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.

The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

Prabowo accepts Raka's resignation

Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.

Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.

Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.

"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."

Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.

"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.

Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.

Long-running allegations over candidacy lead to court disputes

The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.

A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.

The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.

Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.

Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.

Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.

Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.

"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid deepening scandal, leaving AI chip giant at crossroads

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, will not remain on the board.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang looks on during the NVIDIA GTC global AI conference in San Jose, California, US, Mar 17, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Carlos Barria)

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday (Nov 12) after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.

Huang's exit caps a tumultuous week for Nvidia, one of the major engines behind the AI boom, and could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader AI ecosystem, given the ex-CEO's push to preserve access to the Chinese market, as well as his close ties with US President Donald Trump.

The crisis has threatened to implicate some Trump administration members, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is facing growing questions over the administration's oversight of chip sales to China, particularly as both he and Huang pushed for relaxing those sales despite scrutiny from longtime China hawks in both parties. The Commerce Department did not immediately comment.

Senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation told Reuters on Thursday.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lutnick's future. Earlier in the day, a White House official said US President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position."

Huang's departure threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped shape by pouring Nvidia's swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry's biggest labs. The surge in AI computing demand drove a sevenfold increase in Nvidia's shares through early October, pushing its market value at one point to nearly US$6 trillion.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, considering both internal and external candidates, the company said on Thursday.

Who would be next CEO at Nvidia? Top engineer and CFO favoured as candidates

Jensen Huang scandal could spur tighter US scrutiny of AI cloud providers in Southeast Asia: Analysts

The departure has also ignited speculation over who will ultimately lead the company, long associated with the leather-jacket-wearing Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than three decades ago.

Kress and longtime Nvidia engineer Ian Buck had emerged as the leading internal candidates among investors and analysts even before Huang's departure.

Nvidia shares were down about 4.8 per cent, paring earlier losses. Shares of rivals AMD and Broadcom rose about 6 per cent each.

Huang, Nvidia's fourth-largest shareholder with a 3.61 per cent stake, will also leave the board. Nvidia named former Synopsys CEO and longtime director Harvey Jones as its first board chair.

"The Board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period," Kress wrote in a memo to employees, adding that the company will host a meeting on Nov 18.

Kress was gathering Nvidia's executive team at its headquarters on Thursday, CNBC reported, adding that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving.

Huang has hired law firm Paul Weiss, the New York Times reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. It was not clear what the firm had been retained to do, the report said.

The company has not commented beyond its statement announcing Huang's resignation.

REPLACING HUANG

Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

The New York Times also reported Wednesday that Huang had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

While Kress offers investors a familiar hand after 13 years as CFO, analysts have pointed to Buck as a potential longer-term candidate because of Nvidia's reliance on technical leadership. The veteran engineer helped develop its crucial CUDA software platform and now leads its hyperscale AI products.

"The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap ... that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system," said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.

"In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself."

Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.

TRUMP WEIGHS IN

Trump said on Sunday that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country" and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.

Trump had urged Huang to fight for his job in a call on Tuesday, the New York Times reported.

On Thursday, the US president suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over as Nvidia's CEO.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said it was "critically important for right successor to be chosen to replace Huang", noting there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting exports of semiconductor chips to China.

HUANG'S ROCK-STAR STATUS

For years, Nvidia was best known to gamers chasing top-tier graphics. But its chips' ability to perform many calculations at once has made them the oil of the AI boom and a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate the technology. It also made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.

That turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who ask him to sign books, posters and sometimes even their bodies.

The scandal preceding Huang's departure unfolded over more than a year, beginning with an October 2025 New York Times report linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a coveted official Nvidia cloud partner with priority access to its chips.

Subsequent reports said US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang was acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

Washington has also investigated Megaspeed over suspicions it helped China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls, according to media reports.

Alice Huang barred from re-entering Singapore; insufficient evidence she committed offences in Megaspeed probe: MHA

What we know about Megaspeed, Singapore-based customer of Nvidia

Separately, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday that the US Justice Department was investigating Alice Huang over whether entities linked to her were involved in efforts to smuggle Super Micro Computer products to China, citing a person familiar with the matter.

A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office declined to comment on the Bloomberg report. The office previously charged three people associated with Super Micro, including its co-founder, with helping smuggle at least US$2.5 billion of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. Super Micro did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Earlier, the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs said Singapore police had been investigating Super Micro as part of a wider probe into Megaspeed and Alice Huang. The police had reached out to the FBI and the Justice Department for help and had received "limited information or assistance," the ministry said.

Earlier this month, Nvidia's board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.

The controversy escalated on Wednesday when the New York Times reported Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported to him.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday (Nov 12) after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.

Huang's exit caps a tumultuous week for Nvidia, one of the major engines behind the AI boom, and could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader AI ecosystem, given the ex-CEO's push to preserve access to the Chinese market, as well as his close ties with US President Donald Trump.

The crisis has threatened to implicate some Trump administration members, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is facing growing questions over the administration's oversight of chip sales to China, particularly as both he and Huang pushed for relaxing those sales despite scrutiny from longtime China hawks in both parties. The Commerce Department did not immediately comment.
Senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation told Reuters on Thursday.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lutnick's future. Earlier in the day, a White House official said US President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position."

Huang's departure threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped shape by pouring Nvidia's swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry's biggest labs. The surge in AI computing demand drove a sevenfold increase in Nvidia's shares through early October, pushing its market value at one point to nearly US$6 trillion.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, considering both internal and external candidates, the company said on Thursday.

The departure has also ignited speculation over who will ultimately lead the company, long associated with the leather-jacket-wearing Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than three decades ago.
Kress and longtime Nvidia engineer Ian Buck had emerged as the leading internal candidates among investors and analysts even before Huang's departure.
Nvidia shares were down about 4.8 per cent, paring earlier losses. Shares of rivals AMD and Broadcom rose about 6 per cent each.
Huang, Nvidia's fourth-largest shareholder with a 3.61 per cent stake, will also leave the board. Nvidia named former Synopsys CEO and longtime director Harvey Jones as its first board chair.

"The Board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period," Kress wrote in a memo to employees, adding that the company will host a meeting on Nov 18.
Kress was gathering Nvidia's executive team at its headquarters on Thursday, CNBC reported, adding that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving.
Huang has hired law firm Paul Weiss, the New York Times reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. It was not clear what the firm had been retained to do, the report said.
The company has not commented beyond its statement announcing Huang's resignation.
REPLACING HUANG
Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
The New York Times also reported Wednesday that Huang had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

While Kress offers investors a familiar hand after 13 years as CFO, analysts have pointed to Buck as a potential longer-term candidate because of Nvidia's reliance on technical leadership. The veteran engineer helped develop its crucial CUDA software platform and now leads its hyperscale AI products.

"The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap ... that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system," said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.
"In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself."
Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.
TRUMP WEIGHS IN
Trump said on Sunday that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country" and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.
Trump had urged Huang to fight for his job in a call on Tuesday, the New York Times reported.
On Thursday, the US president suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over as Nvidia's CEO.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said it was "critically important for right successor to be chosen to replace Huang", noting there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting exports of semiconductor chips to China.
HUANG'S ROCK-STAR STATUS

For years, Nvidia was best known to gamers chasing top-tier graphics. But its chips' ability to perform many calculations at once has made them the oil of the AI boom and a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate the technology. It also made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.
That turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who ask him to sign books, posters and sometimes even their bodies.

The scandal preceding Huang's departure unfolded over more than a year, beginning with an October 2025 New York Times report linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a coveted official Nvidia cloud partner with priority access to its chips.
Subsequent reports said US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang was acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.
Washington has also investigated Megaspeed over suspicions it helped China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls, according to media reports.

Separately, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday that the US Justice Department was investigating Alice Huang over whether entities linked to her were involved in efforts to smuggle Super Micro Computer products to China, citing a person familiar with the matter.

A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office declined to comment on the Bloomberg report. The office previously charged three people associated with Super Micro, including its co-founder, with helping smuggle at least US$2.5 billion of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. Super Micro did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Earlier, the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs said Singapore police had been investigating Super Micro as part of a wider probe into Megaspeed and Alice Huang. The police had reached out to the FBI and the Justice Department for help and had received "limited information or assistance," the ministry said.

Earlier this month, Nvidia's board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.
The controversy escalated on Wednesday when the New York Times reported Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported to him.

Eight dead after Brooklyn apartment building collapses, NY mayor says

NEW YORK: The death toll from a residential building collapse in New York rose to at least eight, including two children, on Thursday (Nov 12), after more bodies were recovered from the rubble, officials said.

Rescuers worked through the night, searching the site in the Flatbush neighbourhood of Brooklyn where the three-story building collapsed on Wednesday.

They recovered four more bodies overnight, while two others died in the hospital, Fire Chief Lillian Bonsignore told a news conference.

That brought the death toll to eight, including two children, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, adding that another 19 people were injured and one is in critical condition.

"This has been a devastating morning and evening for our city," he said.

Shop worker James Williams, 60, said he witnessed the building collapse after hearing loud banging noises throughout the morning.

"I smelled the smoke from the fumes, and I was watching bricks fall. But to see, like two minutes later, to see the building collapse and fall, it was just devastating," he told AFP.

"There were people trying to get out ... I saw somebody on the side of the staircase, and I'll be honest with you, I didn't even really want to think about that."

Members of the New York City Fire Department and first responders search for victims in the rubble a day after a building collapsed in Brooklyn in New York on Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Charly Triballeau)

Another witness, 14-year-old Kenneilia Reid, told AFP: "When I was walking by, I started seeing dust all of a sudden, and I was like, what is going on? When I turned my back, I saw the whole building collapse."

The building, a three-story structure dating from 1930 with four apartments and a commercial space on the ground floor, collapsed onto a nearby excavation site.

A massive emergency response was launched, with about 250 firefighters and rescue workers and search dogs on site.

An adjacent building was also affected, with one of its walls torn away, leaving a staircase and rooms exposed on the rubble.

The cause of the collapse was not immediately clear, and firefighters continued to work at the site on Thursday.

STOP-WORK ORDER

"My stomach hurts. I can't imagine you were just in your kitchen doing something" and then "you're not any place. It's crazy," Annemarie, a 60-year-old care worker who did not want to share her last name, told AFP. She lives on the street behind the collapsed building.

"It could have been me, you know, it's really scary," she said.

The building fell into an adjacent work site, where construction workers had been excavating, Ahmed Tigani, commissioner of New York's Department of Buildings, told a press conference late Wednesday.

Tigani said that developers had plans approved for a three-story building at the site and were pursuing permission for a nine-story building.

Members of the New York City Fire Department and first responders search for victims in the rubble a day after a building collapsed in Brooklyn in New York on Nov 12, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Charly Triballeau)

According to documents from the city's building department reviewed by AFP, the construction site had been issued a stop-work order in April due to potentially dangerous demolition conditions.

However, work continued, resulting in a US$10,000 fine for the company involved. No link has yet been established between these violations and the building's collapse.

Mamdani said five main entities were involved at the site and authorities on Thursday started "sweeping" 100 other construction sites they are associated with around the city.

The mayor promised a thorough investigation and to hold anyone responsible "fully accountable."

The city's Department of Buildings said its inspectors were on the scene "assisting with recovery operations and conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings."

Source: Reuters/as

SINGAPORE: Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering Singapore after police assessed that she knowingly provided inaccurate information to downplay her role in the company during investigations, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) said on Thursday (Nov 12).

In February 2026, after consulting the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC), police concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.

MHA said that police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing, adding that none of the six people has been in Singapore since investigations began in February 2025.

It added that Huang's passport was returned on Feb 26, 2026, and she left Singapore the same day.

“Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices,” MHA said.

Singapore-based Megaspeed has come under scrutiny following reports that US intelligence officials suspected its former executive Huang of spying for Beijing. Huang is also involved in an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

INVESTIGATIONS INTO MEGASPEED, HUANG

The Singapore Police Force (SPF) and Singapore Customs began an independent investigation in February 2025 into several companies and their key officers over suspected offences involving potential false declarations in the purchase of servers and other related offences.

Megaspeed and its controllers were among those under investigation.

Huang, a Hong Kong resident, was investigated for her suspected involvement in the possible offences in Singapore, given her position as then-CEO, chairperson and one of the key controllers of Megaspeed.

She was not based in Singapore, and was not investigated for espionage, MHA said.

In a press conference on Mar 3, 2025, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs K Shanmugam said that the investigations were not based on any request from any country or sovereign entity.

On Jun 24, 2025, the US Bureau of Industry and Security conducted a voluntary post-shipment verification check at Megaspeed with Huang present. This was the first time Singapore became aware of the US' interest in Megaspeed and Huang.

That same day, SPF interviewed Huang as part of its Megaspeed investigation and impounded her passport to secure her attendance, as she was not based in Singapore.

SERVER EXPORTS THROUGH SINGAPORE

Physical servers had been purchased by companies under investigation and exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market, MHA said.

The police were investigating whether the servers had subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declarations made by the companies in Singapore.

SPF needed to verify the declarations against information and records in other jurisdictions, including the servers' origin and destination jurisdictions.

Singapore therefore sought information from the US and other destination jurisdictions to assist with its independent investigations, the ministry said.

In particular, the police sought information relating to Supermicro, a US-based supplier of servers, which was relevant to its investigations.

After Supermicro provided limited cooperation, SPF and AGC raised this issue with the US authorities at a meeting on Jul 7, 2025, requesting their assistance in securing the company's cooperation.

Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

"Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," MHA said.

ENFORCEMENT ACTION

MHA also said Singapore had charged four individuals and four companies in court between February 2025 and July 2026 for offences including fraud by false representation in relation to the purchase of servers. Fraud by false representation carries a jail term of up to 20 years.

On Feb 27, 2025, three men were charged with fraud in a case involving the alleged movement of servers containing Nvidia chips.

Singaporeans Aaron Woon Guo Jie, 41, and Alan Wei Zhaolun, 49, were charged with criminal conspiracy to commit fraud on a supplier of servers, while Chinese national Li Ming, 51, was charged with fraud by false representation.

On Apr 2, 2026, Singaporean Jenny Lim, 51, was also charged in relation to the same investigation.

Nearly three months later, on Jul 1, police issued a prohibition of disposal order against a Good Class Bungalow valued at around S$55 million and seized about S$1 million in funds in connection with the investigation.

Four companies linked to the individuals - Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech, Aperia Cloud Services and Luxuriate Your Life - were also charged with related fraud offences.

Wei later faced fresh money-laundering charges on Jul 6, including one accusing him of laundering S$38 million in alleged criminal proceeds through the purchase of an S$55 million bungalow, bringing the total number of charges against him to 11.

SINGAPORE'S POSITION ON EXPORT CONTROLS

MHA said while Singapore does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, it expects all companies operating here to take into account such regulations, including export controls, in their international business activities.

"Singapore does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries’ export controls through fraud or dishonest practices," it said.

"Our approach is clear. Singapore will conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available.

"We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."

MEGASPEED WILL COOPERATE WITH US AUTHORITIES

Earlier on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO and chairman James Tan Yong Pong said: "Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government.”

In the statement posted on the company's website, Tan said Megaspeed had cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security and "stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant US government authority".

Megaspeed has also retained a leading US law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its graphics processing units and independently verify its export control compliance practices, he said.

"Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable US laws," Tan added.

At noon on Nov 11, CNA attempted to visit Megaspeed’s office at Ocean Financial Centre, but was stopped by the building’s staff.

Megaspeed’s office is located on the seventh floor of the commercial building in Collyer Quay.

The director of Megaspeed is identified as Tan Yong Pong, according to Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) filings.

Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International before changing its name to Megaspeed International in March 2023.

Publicly available data also shows that Tan is also the director and sole shareholder of Swiftdata, the holding company that wholly owns Megaspeed.

CNA also visited Swiftdata’s office at Block 26 Sin Ming Lane later in the afternoon, which appeared to be unoccupied.

Ringing the doorbell at the fourth-floor unit at the Midview City business park brought no response.

Workers from a neighbouring unit told CNA that Swiftdata’s office is usually shut.

On Feb 27, 2025, three men were charged with fraud in a case involving the alleged movement of servers containing Nvidia chips.

Singaporeans Aaron Woon Guo Jie, 41, and Alan Wei Zhaolun, 49, were charged with criminal conspiracy to commit fraud on a supplier of servers, while Chinese national Li Ming, 51, was charged with fraud by false representation.
On Apr 2, 2026, Singaporean Jenny Lim, 51, was also charged in relation to the same investigation.

Nearly three months later, on Jul 1, police issued a prohibition of disposal order against a Good Class Bungalow valued at around S$55 million and seized about S$1 million in funds in connection with the investigation.
Four companies linked to the individuals - Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech, Aperia Cloud Services and Luxuriate Your Life - were also charged with related fraud offences.

MHA said while Singapore does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, it expects all companies operating here to take into account such regulations, including export controls, in their international business activities.
"Singapore does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries’ export controls through fraud or dishonest practices," it said.
"Our approach is clear. Singapore will conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available.
"We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."
MEGASPEED WILL COOPERATE WITH US AUTHORITIES

Earlier on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO and chairman James Tan Yong Pong said: "Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government.”

In the statement posted on the company's website, Tan said Megaspeed had cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security and "stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant US government authority".
Megaspeed has also retained a leading US law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its graphics processing units and independently verify its export control compliance practices, he said.

"Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable US laws," Tan added.

Metro Bank has been focused on a turnaround plan since it was forced into the £925m rescue deal in 2023. Photograph: John Keeble/Getty Images

Metro Bank up for sale, with billionaire investor in line for £420m windfall

Shares up 7% after announcement as Jaime Gilinski Bacal seeks exit three years after helping to rescue bank

Metro Bank is putting itself up for sale three years after its near-collapse, in a move that could hand a £420m windfall to its Colombian billionaire investor, Jaime Gilinski Bacal.

Metro Bank made the rare decision to publicly announce it was open to bids on Thursday, paving the way for a wider pool of suitors. The announcement pushed the share price up by 7% by mid-morning, valuing the bank at about £1.3bn.

If successful, the sale would allow Gilinski Bacal a chance to sell out of the bank he helped save from near-failure in late 2023.

The 68-year-old banking tycoon, who took a seat on Metro’s board after securing a 53% stake three years ago, has already seen a sixfold increase in the value of his shares, which he bought for just 30p each as part of a wider rescue deal. That means that at Thursday’s 190p share price, his British Virgin Island-based vehicle Spaldy Investments, could cash out with a £427m windfall.

It would mark the latest turnaround success for the billionaire, who made his fortune snapping up assets of struggling lenders on the cheap, before overhauling their operations and selling them on for a big profit. Gilinski Bacal is one of the wealthiest people in Latin America, worth about $16.9bn (£12.7bn), according to Forbes.

Gilinski Bacal took a seat on Metro’s board after securing a 53% stake three years ago and has seen a sixfold increase in the value of his shares. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Metro Bank has been focused on a turnaround plan – which has involved lending more heavily to businesses and people with more erratic incomes – since it was forced into the £925m rescue deal in 2023.

Metro was the first high street bank to open in the UK in more than 100 years when it was launched by another billionaire, the US businessman Vernon Hill, in 2010. It attracted a wave of customers, and offered dog-friendly branches with seven-day openings.

However, it struggled after a major accounting blunder in 2019 that prompted investors to dump their shares and fearful customers to pull their cash. It led to the resignation of top executives, as well as the then chair, Hill, who was well-known for having his yorkshire terrier Sir Duffy (and later Sir Duffy II) in tow.

Metro’s shares took another dive in 2023. That year, it emerged that the bank would need more cash from investors, having failed to convince regulators that it could be trusted to assess its own risks.

The 2019 accounting blunder led to the resignations of top executives as well as the then chair, Vernon Hill. Photograph: John Stillwell/PA

The lender finally secured a rescue, which was brokered in part by UK regulators at the Bank of England, in 2023. It has since embarked on the turnaround plan, which has increased its profits but came at a cost for staff and customers. Metro’s chief executive, Daniel Frumkin, slashed more than 1,000 jobs in spring 2024 and decided to close branches on Sundays.

The bank said on Thursday that a sale was just one of the options on the table and that it would still be able to go it alone if no suitable bidder came through.

Metro’s board “unanimously believes that evaluating potential interest in the company” through a potential sale “will maximise the value creation opportunities available to shareholders and deliver benefits for all stakeholders”, the bank said.

One of the wards destroyed in the strike on Nasser hospital in Gaza, which Israel said was targeting Hamas fighters. Photograph: Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu/Getty Images

Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in Gaza kills surgeon and five others

Hospital director says 28 wounded in attack on one of few remaining medical facilities in the strip

An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The Israeli military carried out the attack on the hospital, in Khan Younis, early on Thursday saying in a statement it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters there, without providing evidence.

The strike destroyed part of the surgery department, and caused extensive damage to several floors. Services were suspended in four departments: radiology, laboratories, surgical operations and inpatient surgical wards, according to Dr Ahmed al-Fara, hospital director.

The ceiling of one of the wards had caved in, while debris-covered beds lay next to medical instruments twisted from the force of the blast. In other rooms, piles of rubble and shattered concrete cluttered the floor and a hole was left in the floor, where the bomb penetrated the building.

Women mourn during the funeral of patients killed during the strike on Nasser hospital on Thursday. Photograph: Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu/Getty Images

Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist at Nasser medical complex, who was wounded in the attack, said: “The bombing caused thick smoke to fill the rooms and fires to break out, amid the groans of wounded and people’s screams. There were many casualties and blood everywhere … Most of us sustained injuries to our limbs, as well as shrapnel wounds in different parts of our bodies.”

Ubaid said the strike came at about 12.30am, without warning. “The patients in the department were all surgical patients waiting to undergo operations. The bombing happened at a time when they should have been asleep,” he said.

Among the dead was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had featured in American Doctor, a documentary about doctors operating in Gaza.

“Dr Rizk was in the American Doctor documentary operating and serving his people. He lost his life doing that, he lost his life because he was doing that,” Dr Thaer Ahmad, who also featured in the documentary, posted on X.

Abu Shaira was killed alongside one of his patients, on whom he had operated.

Nasser hospital is one of the last functioning healthcare facilities in Gaza, after Israeli bombing made most of the strip’s facilities unusable. Last year Israel also struck the hospital, killing five journalists in a double-tap strike on a location often used by reporters for filming. In all, the hospital has been attacked seven times since the war on Gaza began.

map

The Israeli military has accused Hamas of using hospitals as command centres and to store weapons, an accusation the militant movement rejects. More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed in Gaza, while Doctors Without Borders (MSF) says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since 7 October 2023, with at least 95 still in custody.

About 90% of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damage by Israeli bombing, systematic destruction UN experts called “medicide”.

Attacking healthcare facilities and staff is illegal under international humanitarian law, though these facilities can lose their protected status if they are used for military purposes.

There is an increased need for healthcare during the winter months in Gaza, where rains have displaced people from their tents and increased communicable diseases in crowded encampments.

Already, Nasser hospital is lacking about 80% of its essential medicines and medical supplies, said al-Fara, its director.

One of those killed in Thursday’s strike was Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, who was admitted to Nasser hospital on Monday after a piece of debris fell on his back while he was helping clear rubble from a friend’s home. He was scheduled for surgery at 10am on Thursday, and was meant to receive further treatment abroad.

“Seif was a young man in the prime of his life. He wanted to live, rebuild his home and start a normal life, free from problems and suffering … Seif was killed after already losing two of his brothers and his father. His mother has now lost three of her sons,” said his cousin Tareq Abu Hatab, 37.

A view of the destruction in Nasser hospital on Thursday. Photograph: Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu/Getty Images

Israel launched the war in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostage. At least 74,645 people have since been killed in Gaza and Israel has carried out a genocide in the strip, according to the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

Israel continues to carry out airstrikes in Gaza, killing more than 1,600 people since the October 2025 “ceasefire”, according to the Gaza ministry of health.
